Note · Kotter — Leading Change

3 min read777 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-kotter-leading-change.md

Canon · Cluster: Culture & Change · Maps to E5 (Transformation & Change Management)

  • Source: John Kotter, Leading Change (1996)
  • Core claim: Change fails for predictable reasons — and it fails on emotion, not logic. You need both the analytical argument and the emotional case.
  • Framework — the eight steps: 1. Create a sense of urgency. 2. Build a guiding coalition. 3. Form a strategic vision (and strategy). 4. Enlist a volunteer army (communicate the vision relentlessly). 5. Remove barriers / enable action. 6. Generate short-term wins. 7. Sustain acceleration — don't let up. 8. Institute change (anchor it in culture).
  • The two classic killers: insufficient urgency at the start, and declaring victory too early (step 7).
  • Applies when: leading a large, deliberate organizational transformation that needs broad buy-in over a long horizon.
  • Breaks when: it's a linear, top-down, big-bang model — it fits slow industrial change far better than continuous, iterative, or bottom-up change, where Heath's "shrink the change" and Switch's environment-design beat an 8-step program (canon heath switch). "Create urgency" is routinely faked into manufactured crisis, which breeds cynicism. And step 8 (anchor in culture) collides with Schein's truth that you can't simply install assumptions (canon schein organizational culture) — the model under-prices how slow that last step is.
  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-05 — r/managers + Kotter-model transcripts) The corpus confirms Kotter's emotion-over-logic thesis from the failure side. r/managers' "The 'silent resignation' nobody notices" (9,404↑) names the exact mechanism behind a stalled coalition: a great employee "stops pushing… No more bold ideas," and "it usually happens after too many ignored ideas, decisions made without them or endless urgent work that kills anything meaningful." That is a step-6 failure — no visible wins, no progress, so the volunteer army starves. "Got them a raise. They used it to quit." (2,923↑) shows the same: an analytical fix (comp correction) with no emotional engagement just funds the exit. Kotter International itself reframes the model around this: "there's so much research that shows motivation really comes from progress… the more success we have along the way, the more momentum we build" — short-term wins aren't a checkbox, they're the fuel.
  • Researched layer (2026-06-05)
  • Canonical explanation (sourced): the model's engine is urgency built on feeling, not data. The animated summary states it flatly: "you can't appeal to people with data and facts alone you must also account for how people feel… this step is all about igniting the hearts and minds of your people" (BigIdeasGrowingMinds). EPM adds the operational threshold Kotter set — "a minimum of 75 percent of management needs to back an initiative… for it to be successful" — so urgency is shared belief, not an announcement.
  • Real application (mined): the corpus' clearest live case is the inverse of step 6. In r/managers' "silent resignation" thread (9,404↑) a high performer goes quiet "after too many ignored ideas… and endless urgent work that kills anything meaningful" — i.e., all manufactured urgency, zero short-term wins. The fix Kotter prescribes (step 4 enlist + step 6 wins) is exactly what the manager describes missing: people who "want to help make this change a reality," not "somebody else should do it" (Kotter International).
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: practitioners flag the model's top-down blind spot. EPM's own teardown lists the disadvantages: "it's a top-down model so you can miss potential opportunities because not everyone is involved in the co-creation of the vision… and while the model is really good for initiating change it doesn't help you as much when it comes to sustaining change." Kotter International quietly concedes this, recasting the "8 steps" as "eight accelerators… not a linear process" run in parallel — an admission the original big-bang sequencing was too rigid.

Take a change you're trying to drive. Which of the 8 steps have you actually done? Most stalls are a missing step 1 (real urgency) or a premature step 7 (declaring victory). Name yours.
